title: Bhopal, 23 July 1955: How the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh began
author: Editorial Desk
summary: A small gathering in Bhopal, a birth anniversary of Lokmanya Tilak, and a union with not one registered affiliate.
body:
Most large organisations start with a split from an older one. The Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh did not. It began on **23 July 1955** at Bhopal, when a small group of invitees from different parts of the country met and announced a new national trade union centre. What makes the story worth telling is not the date alone but how little there was on that day, and how much was built afterwards.

## The setting: a labour movement tied to politics

To understand why BMS was started, one has to picture the labour movement of the early 1950s. The established central trade union organisations of that period were closely linked to political parties or political groups. BMS's own history, *The Onward March of BMS*, describes the new body as a reaction to two things: "political unionism", in which unions serve the interests of a party, and what it calls "bread-butter unionism", which concerns itself only with economic gains for members.

BMS's founders wanted something different. They argued that workers' interests had to be pursued within the interests of the nation, and that society is a third and more important party in industrial relations, besides the employer and the worker. They did not accept the idea of class conflict as the basis of the labour movement. Instead they spoke of a "vertical" arrangement of society and of cooperation between its parts, while rejecting both capitalism and communism.

## Why 23 July

BMS records that 23 July was chosen because it is the birth anniversary of **Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak**, the veteran of the freedom movement, and the founding is described as having taken place on Tilak Jayanti. The founding is associated with **Dattopant Thengadi**, a Sangh pracharak who had already spent years working among labour. Biographical accounts say that in 1950-51 he served as an organising secretary of the INTUC, the Congress-linked union centre, which gave him a close look at how existing unions functioned.

## Starting from zero

The most striking fact in BMS's own account is how it began. *The Onward March of BMS* notes that on the day of its founding BMS did not have a single registered union affiliated to it and "had to begin from the scratch". BMS's website says the same thing in different words: no union, no members, no activists, no office and no funds. Another tribute written by a former BMS leader describes the ambition of building a large organisation from nothing at a time when communist-led unions were strong.

The method that followed was slow. According to the same history, unions were built from the bottom up: first local unions, then larger unions, then state federations and state units, and finally national industrial federations. There was no all-India executive in the early years. The first all-India convention came only after about twelve years, and it was at that convention that a National Executive was elected for the first time. Before that, BMS had no National Executive or all-India office-bearers.

## The first conference and the first office-bearers

BMS's website states that its first all-India conference was held in **Delhi in 1967**, twelve years after its founding. At that conference the organisation reported 541 affiliated unions. The site also gives a membership figure for 1967 that appears in slightly different forms on the page, so readers who need an exact number should check the primary document. The same page records that Thengadi was the first General Secretary and Babasaheb Kamble the first President.

Those twelve years were not easy. The history describes early activists facing employer victimisation, government hostility and opposition from established unions. Many of the early karyakartas were social workers with little experience of trade unions. They learnt by doing, one workplace at a time.

## Standing with workers in big struggles

It would be wrong to think that a constructive approach meant staying away from struggle. The same history records BMS's participation in major labour actions. It lists the 1963 Bombay Bundh, in which BMS acted as coordinator, and the 1974 railway strike, in which it took part as a constituent of the National Coordination Committee for Railwaymen's Struggle. The organisation's position, then and since, has been that the right to strike is recognised, but that agitation should be constructive and should not be the only method a union knows.

## Growth and recognition

How large BMS is depends on whose count one reads and when. The BMS website reports the following from Government verification exercises:

- A membership verification in 1984 ranked BMS as the second-largest central trade union organisation, with 12,11,355 members.
- In 1996 the Ministry of Labour declared it the largest, with 31,17,324 members; the website notes that the reckoning date for that exercise was 31 December 1989.
- A verification in 2002 kept it in first place.

The history document cited above, which appears to be from an earlier period, gives a lower figure and a different ranking, which is a reminder that these numbers changed over time and were counted for different dates. Today BMS says it has affiliates in all 44 industries classified by the Ministry of Labour and nearly one crore members, with more than 5,000 affiliated unions. A 2025 article in *Organiser*, a publication close to the movement, gives about 6,500 affiliated unions and says BMS is active in more than 620 districts. These are claims by the organisation and its sympathisers rather than independently audited counts, and should be read that way.

## Why Bhopal still matters

The Bhopal story carries a lesson for anyone who works in an organisation. A declaration can be made in an afternoon. What cannot be made in an afternoon is a union that workers trust, and that takes years of patient work at the base: a first union in one factory, a federation of such unions, a representative who is willing to go to the workplace and listen. BMS often says that its strength comes from that kind of work, and its history is consistent with that claim.

It also explains the organisation's character. Because BMS began without help from any party, it has regularly described itself as independent of political parties, while still being willing to work with governments of any colour. It speaks of "responsive cooperation": supporting what it finds good in a government's measures and opposing what it finds harmful to workers.

## What comes next

In coming weeks this blog will look at the thinking behind that founding, the three-line motto and the phrase *Rashtra hit, Udyog hit, Mazdoor hit*, and the life of Dattopant Thengadi. Together these posts will show how an organisation that started without a single union became a major presence in Indian labour.
